title: Cancer Alley residents face rising cancer risk from clustered industrial emissions
description: New analysis maps how 150 petrochemical plants clustered along an 85-mile stretch of Louisiana drive elevated cancer risk in predominantly Black communities.

content_html:
ST. JAMES PARISH, Louisiana — Along an 85-mile corridor that follows the Mississippi River between New Orleans and Baton Rouge, more than 150 petrochemical plants and refineries operate in one of the densest concentrations of heavy industry in the Western Hemisphere. Residents of this strip, known as Cancer Alley, breathe air that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has repeatedly flagged for elevated concentrations of toxic compounds including ethylene oxide, chloroprene, and benzene.

The demographic composition of the corridor is not accidental. In parishes such as St. John the Baptist and St. James, predominantly Black communities live within the fence lines of facilities that did not exist when their families settled the land generations ago. OzoneNews's community impact desk is mapping where the health data and the industrial footprint overlap.

The EPA Cancer-Risk Math | What Air Toxics Data Actually Shows

The EPA's National Air Toxics Assessment is the agency's primary tool for estimating the cancer risk a community faces from breathing industrial air. Three-year screening data covering the corridor consistently ranks sections of Louisiana's industrial parishes near the top of the agency's risk tiers. In several census tracts straddling the river, modeled lifetime excess cancer risk from air toxics runs many times higher than the national average for the surrounding state and region.

Ethylene oxide, used to sterilize medical equipment and manufacture antifreeze and plastics, is classified by the EPA as a known human carcinogen. Chloroprene, a feedstock in the production of synthetic rubber, was the subject of a high-profile enforcement action against a Denka Performance Elastomer facility in St. John the Baptist Parish, where the EPA found community-level exposures above levels the agency considers safe over a lifetime.

The public health desk has reported on how air toxics interact with existing health disparities, compounding risk in communities with reduced access to preventive care.

The Cumulative Burden | Multiple Plants, One Airshed

Individual permits rarely account for the whole picture. Each facility is typically permitted on its own, but residents of Cancer Alley do not breathe emissions from one plant at a time. They are exposed to a combined plume from dozens of operating units across an airshed that shares the same river valley, wind, and weather patterns.

Environmental health researchers describe this as the cumulative impact problem. The EPA's EJScreen mapping tool, introduced to model environmental burden by census block group, shows that the corridor's demographic indicators such as percentage of people of color and income sit in high percentiles nationally, while particulate matter and air toxics cancer risk indicators also track high. It is the overlap of these two rankings that defines the environmental justice case.

Community advocates in St. James Parish have fought for years to block new construction, most prominently a proposed Formosa Plastics complex that would add a massive new petrochemical footprint to an already saturated airshed. The legal and permitting disputes around that single project became a national flashpoint for the broader debate over whether new heavy industry belongs in communities already carrying disproportionate pollution load. The ethics desk has covered the accountability gap between permitting agencies and the communities they are meant to protect.

What Comes Next | Science, Litigation, and the Right to Breathe

The trajectory of Cancer Alley hinges on three fronts. First, the EPA's ongoing review of ethylene oxide under the Clean Air Act has tightened the standard for what the agency considers an acceptable lifetime risk from a single pollutant. Second, a series of civil-rights complaints filed under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act argue that Louisiana's permitting practices impose a discriminatory burden on Black residents, a legal theory that has forced the EPA to open investigations into state environmental agencies. Third, community-led air monitoring networks are now collecting their own data, reducing reliance on industry and agency estimates.

For residents who have lived in the shadow of these plants for decades, the question is not whether the risk exists, but whether the institutions with authority to act will finally treat their air as a civil right. Follow the OzoneNews community desk as this reporting continues.
